chhau.title: The Science of Chhau Dance
chhau.body:
I learned the choreography before I understood the dance.

This book is my attempt to go back, look again, and ask what Chhau is doing inside the body, the music, the mask, and the space.

Arnav Ajana

about-me.title: I Performed It Before I Understood It
about-me.body:
The first time I learned Chhau, I was preparing for an international dance competition.

At that point, it was choreography. I had to remember the sequence, hold the formation, arrive on the beat, and make the movement look convincing. I was so focused on performing it correctly that I did not stop to ask where those movements came from.

But Chhau did not leave when the competition ended.

During later school rehearsals, my friends and I kept returning to its movements, even when we were meant to be practising something else. We were not discussing history or technique. We simply liked the way the movement felt: grounded, sharp, powerful, and strangely difficult to forget.

That was when I realised something uncomfortable. I had performed Chhau, but I could not properly explain what I had performed.

Why was the Mayurbhanj tradition unmasked? What were the drums telling the dancer? Why did three traditions share one name while looking so different? Were the movement names I had learned used everywhere, or only by one teacher?

This book began with those questions. I am not a Chhau guru or historian. I am a dancer returning to a form I met too quickly, trying to understand it more honestly through practitioners, performances, books, recordings, and the body itself.

why-this-book-exists.title: The Book I Needed at the Beginning
why-this-book-exists.body:
When I first searched for Chhau, I found two kinds of material.

Some sources gave me history, names, and dates, but the movement stayed trapped inside paragraphs. Other sources gave me extraordinary performances, but did not always tell me which movement I was seeing, what the rhythm was doing, or how the three traditions differed.

I wanted one place where a beginner could **see the body, hear the music, meet the people, and then follow the evidence**.

That is what this eBook is trying to become.

A photograph can show the height of a Purulia crown. It cannot show how a dancer prepares for a turn. A written definition can name _chauk_. It cannot show how weight travels through the feet, knees, pelvis, and chest. A drum can be listed in a glossary, but until we hear it beside movement, we do not understand its job.

The first version of this book relied too heavily on text and prototype models. That was not enough. Wherever movement is central, the finished edition needs practitioner-approved video: front view, side view, normal speed, slow motion, spoken terminology, rhythm, preparation, action, and recovery.

The screen still cannot replace a teacher. But it can help a beginner arrive at the teacher with better eyes and better questions.

what-science-means.title: Why I Use the Word “Science”
what-science-means.body:
I am not using the word _science_ to make Chhau sound more impressive. I use it because the dance gives us real questions about how bodies, materials, sound, and space work together.

What happens to balance when the stance becomes wider and lower? How does a dancer shift weight without losing readiness? What changes when the face is covered by a mask? How do heat, restricted vision, headgear, costume, and a large performance ground affect movement? How does a drum cue prepare the body before the audience sees the action?

These are questions we can investigate through close observation, comparison, measurement where suitable, and honest limits.

This book therefore looks at five connected systems:

- **Body:** balance, weight transfer, direction, preparation, force, rhythm, breath, and recovery.
- **Sound:** pulse, tempo, cue, accent, melody, and the exchange between dancer and musician.
- **Material:** how masks, costumes, ornaments, and props change visibility, effort, silhouette, and motion.
- **Space:** how an akhara, open arena, entrance path, stage, and audience reshape performance.
- **Evidence:** who made a claim, where it applies, what another source says, and what remains uncertain.

This is not a laboratory trial, a medical guide, or proof that a movement is safe or therapeutic. It is a way of looking carefully and refusing to pretend that a beautiful answer is automatically a true one.

how-to-use-this-book.title: How to Read, Watch, and Listen
how-to-use-this-book.body:
You can read this book from the beginning, but you do not have to treat it like a textbook.

Each page asks you to do one of four things:

- **Watch:** follow a real performance or a practitioner-approved demonstration.
- **Listen:** notice a drum, reed instrument, cue, accent, or change in tempo.
- **Look closer:** use a photograph, diagram, map, or 3D study to inspect one detail.
- **Think:** compare two explanations and decide what the evidence actually supports.

When a movement video is added, watch it once without reading. Then watch again for the feet, knees, pelvis, chest, head, gaze, rhythm, and recovery. A spectacular airborne moment is never the whole movement. Preparation and landing matter just as much.

The 3D viewer is useful for turning a held shape and studying the line from another angle. It is not a teacher, and a frozen model cannot explain timing.

Numbered citations open the source library. They are there for readers who want to check a statement or continue beyond my explanation.

> Watch: The movement pages in Chapters 4 and 5 now state exactly which filmed views are still needed. Until those demonstrations are reviewed, the page will tell you what to notice rather than pretending to teach the step.

promise-to-the-reader.title: What I Will and Will Not Pretend
promise-to-the-reader.body:
I will not pretend that Chhau becomes simple because it is on a screen.

If two sources disagree, I will show the disagreement. If a word changes between regions or teachers, I will not quietly choose one version and call it universal. If a model has not been reviewed by a practitioner, it will be labelled as a prototype rather than presented as tradition.

I will also separate **watching** from **training**.

Chhau asks for strength, stamina, coordination, repetition, and correction. Deep stances, leaps, turns, falls, masked movement, acrobatics, and weapon phrases belong with a qualified teacher. A video can help us observe preparation and recovery. It cannot judge your body, fatigue, injury history, floor, or surroundings.

A second promise is about people. Dancers, gurus, musicians, makers, troupes, researchers, and communities are not background material for this project. Their names, permissions, regional traditions, and knowledge must travel with every image, recording, model, and explanation.

This book is not an attempt to own Chhau. It is an attempt to meet it with more care than I did the first time.

map-of-chhau.title: Begin With Three Places
map-of-chhau.body:
Before comparing masks or movements, place the three traditions on the map.

Mayurbhanj Chhau is centred in Mayurbhanj district in northern Odisha. Seraikella Chhau is centred in Seraikella in present-day Jharkhand. Purulia Chhau is practised across Purulia district in West Bengal. [1][2][7][11][12]

They are close enough for people, instruments, stories, and movement ideas to travel. They are also rooted in different local histories. That combination—exchange and difference—is one of the most important ideas in this book.

UNESCO inscribed Chhau dance in 2010, and the inscription includes all three traditions. [1]

Use the atlas first to find Baripada, Seraikella, and Purulia. Then open another marker and ask a simple question: **What exactly does this source prove?**

> Look: Geography is not decoration here. Distance, borders, travel, patronage, festivals, and local communities all help explain why the three traditions are related without becoming the same.

first-look.title: Look at the Body Before the Costume
first-look.body:
The first thing many people notice in Chhau is the mask or costume. I did too.

Now I try to look in a different order.

First, I follow the base of the body: the distance between the feet, the bend of the knees, and where the weight appears to settle. Then I look at the chest, head, direction of focus, and the pathway through space. Only after that do I return to the mask, crown, ornaments, or prop.

This changes what I see.

Mayurbhanj leaves the face uncovered, but the body still carries most of the meaning. Seraikella uses a fixed mask, yet a small change in head angle or torso shape can change how that face appears. Purulia may create an enormous silhouette, but scale should not hide technique.

> Look: Hide the face in a photograph or model for a moment. What can you already understand from stance, direction, rhythm, and silhouette?

The prototype figures on this page are useful only for practising viewpoint and comparison. They are not evidence of a real Chhau costume, character, jump, or regional technique.
